title: The Emotions of Fortitude
description: Giordano, “Allegory of Prudence, 1682, via Wikimedia Commons. What is Fortitude? Fortitude, or courage, is a virtue that enables us to face significant threats and overcome significant obstacles to our good. A common supposed image of fortitude today might involve a fearless superhero in the face of a foe or a fearful but determined soldier in the face of the enemy. But we cannot tell simply from what a person does whether he or she acts with fortitude. In fact, the superhero may not have fortitude at all while the soldier may. The reason is that fortitude requires fear. This may surprise you given it is common today for fearlessness to be held up as the ideal in facing danger. But St. Thomas knows better. Fortitude, in its primary sense, involves facing threats that may result in our death or serious injury. Fear is a natural response when facing the greatest threats to our life or what we love most. Fortitude controls and harnesses fear, and other emotions as well, to face the threats. These other emotions are hope and daring . For Aquinas, fear and daring are contrary emotions. This means that we cannot have them at the same time regarding the same object. This raises a puzzle. How can a single virtue require two contrary emotions? Isn’t that impossible? Thanks for reading Investigations by the Thomistic Institute! Subscribe for free to receive new posts in your inbox every Monday. Fortitude and the Stages of a Prudent Human Act To answer this question, and to show the place of the emotion of hope as well, we’ve got to think about human action. In his discussion of prudence , St. Thomas writes, Prudence is right reason applied to action , as stated above (A. 2).

title: Anger: A Good or an Evil?
description: By Fr. Basil Cole, O.P., and Fr. John Baptist Ku, O.P. Bernardino Mei, “Christ Cleansing the Temple,” 1655, via WikiMedia Commons. What is anger? Scripture seems to suggest that anger is an evil. For instance, we read, “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Mt 5:22), and “Now put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and foul talk from your mouth” (Col 3:8). But St. Thomas Aquinas clarifies that “to be angry is not always an evil. ” To explain, Thomas borrows the words of St. John Chrysostom: A man who is angry without cause is guilty, but not he that is angry with cause, for without anger sound doctrine would not be advanced or good judgment maintained or crime put down. “Anger” names a passion and a vice. The passion of anger is good in itself, but it can be excessive or deficient. When it is had with the right intensity for the right length of time, it is virtuous. Otherwise, it is disordered. The vice of anger is a stable disposition to have the passion of anger in excess. All vices are defects of moral character from which sinful actions flow. The passions work together with the will, which works together with the intellect. You can think of the intellect like a lame man, the will like a blind man who is carrying the lame man, and the passions like dogs leashed to the blind man’s belt. The intellect sees but cannot move; it relies on the will to move. The will moves, but it cannot see; it relies on intellect to see. And the passions make movement easier or harder. When the passions are well-trained, they are like well-trained dogs that can make walking up a steep hill effortless. Conversely, when they are disobedient, they can pull you to the ground.

title: Thomas Aquinas on Meekness
description: Thomas Aquinas on Meekness Nowadays, the concept of meekness gets a bad rap. As I’ve argued elsewhere , though, meekness, far from being a weakness, is a character strength . In this post, I say a bit about why that is, and how St. Thomas Aquinas understood the undersung virtue of meekness. Let me start with a few illustrations, priming your pump. You no doubt know people whose anger is a liability. Maybe you’ve coached a player who, when enticed, would commit a technical or unsportsmanlike penalty. Maybe you remember how you could turn the tide of any argument with a sibling by baiting her into rash overreactions. You could have a hotheaded friend that you are apprehensive of going out with, for fear that he’ll challenge the whole bar to a fight. Or maybe you’ve watched a student enrage a flustered teacher to the point where she screams, much to the delight of a filming co-conspirator. In each of these four cases, there’s a shared liability: anger gets the best of the player, sibling, friend, and teacher. An engrained disposition to be overtaken by anger is an unbecoming feature. The other team, if they know his predilections, will try to exploit those liabilities. Even if he is the best at his position, his coach might still bench him, for fear that his wrath will cost them the game. And while you can’t quite bench a friend, you might forget to invite him out if you want a peaceful night. Nobody wants a wildcard. It is no doubt because of the moral liabilities that come with unchecked anger that scripture says, “He who is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city” (Proverbs 16:32).
